title: From Facts to Frameworks
author: Kurt Wootton
summary: Kurt Wootton opens with a school presentation on the Dominican Republic in which students recited exports and music but could not name the neighbouring country on the island or the Trujillo dictatorship, and uses it to ask what students really need to know in a subject. He rejects the either/or fight between knowledge-based and experiential teaching and argues skilled teachers weave both. His planning process has three steps: identify about five essential facts, let those facts raise questions, and use the questions to reach an intellectual framework, an interconnected set of ideas students can apply to new subjects. He separates frameworks from Wiggins and McTighe's enduring understandings, and illustrates with symbolism in The Great Gatsby, parabolas built into rockets at High Tech High Mesa, and photosynthesis leading to how living systems transform energy. Drawing on David Perkins' warning about elementitis, he insists the aim is students who know more, can think with big ideas, and want to use them well.
points: Essential facts are a floor, not a ceiling: students should leave knowing a handful of key facts, but a unit that stops there is the Gradgrind model.
A framework is a transferable set of connected ideas, such as how dictatorships rise and fall or how symbolism works, which is narrower and more usable than a general enduring understanding.
The facts, questions, frameworks sequence gives teachers a planning routine, and older students can make choosing the essential facts itself a research task.
The High Tech High parabola rockets show the knowledge and experiential camps combining: students practised equations and then used them to model a real trajectory.
Perkins' idea of elementitis names the failure of teaching the pieces of a subject without ever letting students see the whole game.
quotes: I believe we can have the best of both worlds. Skilled teachers weave these practices together into a rich tapestry of reading, thinking, writing, and doing.

Those essential facts are important, but they are only a means to the end. What is also critical, and often missing from classrooms, are the “intellectual frameworks” necessary for understanding the central ideas of a given subject area.
I feel like much of what is missing from education is students learning not just skills and facts, but how to build and work with intellectual frameworks.

An enduring understanding is an important idea we want students to remember long after a unit has ended. An intellectual framework is an interconnected set of ideas students can use to understand new subjects and systems.

What we do need for them to understand is how writers, painters, filmmakers, songwriters use symbolism in storytelling. When is an object a symbol and when is it only an object? How as viewers or readers can we know?

He explains that the way we often teach is like teaching the rules of baseball without ever letting students play the game. He refers to the concept of “elementitis” as teaching the pieces of a subject without ever letting students experience the whole
The goal is to move from a group of facts (important, but not the end in themselves) to ways of thinking that help us understand the larger world.

We want students to leave our classrooms knowing more about the world around them, with the intellectual frameworks to make sense of that knowledge, and the desire to use what they've learned to make the world a better place.
